title: RTPproxy: Fix malformed-packet bugs and catch up with the protocol
description:
The RTPproxy dissector had drifted a long way from what RTPproxy and
rtpengine actually speak, and several framing bugs made it report
ordinary traffic as malformed.

Fixes first, then protocol coverage, then the RTPproxy-ng (bencode)
side. Each commit stands alone and builds.

### Malformed-packet fixes

* `tvb_find_uint8_length()` was given an absolute offset where it wants
  a byte count, at all three call sites. The searches ran to the end of
  the captured data, and **every session command carrying a tag — D, R,
  N, U, L, P, C, Q — was reported as `[Malformed Packet]`**, because the
  zero-length Media-ID placeholder ended up anchored outside the tvb.
* The second tag was recomputed from a stale offset, so
  `D call_id from_tag to_tag` printed `from_tag` twice and never showed
  the to_tag. Without a to_tag it fell through to the notification
  parser and reported the from_tag as a notify target.
* The whole argument path walked with unbounded searches and never
  compared against the end of the command, so a command with fewer
  arguments than its syntax allows ran past its own end and wrapped
  `end - begin`. `U call_id 192.168.0.1 10000` was enough — and a
  truncated control datagram is not a rare thing.
* The `P` and `U` modifiers consumed a byte without checking one was
  there; `CP call_id target from_tag` was malformed.

Over a corpus of 1604 generated commands this takes the number of
dissector exceptions from **969 to zero**.

### Protocol coverage

`G` (get statistics) and `N` (stop recording) were not recognised at
all — such packets showed a bare cookie and took no part in
request/reply tracking. Also added: the `&&` sub-command trailer, which
the positional parser previously ate as a tag; the `Q` command's counter
names and its reply, decoded into typed per-counter fields
(`rtpproxy.counter.ndropped` and friends) so they can be filtered and
graphed; IPv6 and `{label}` forms of the `L`/`R` modifiers; the `unix:`,
`tcp:` and bare-path notify socket forms, which used to be run through
the IPv4 parser and reported as bad addresses; the `v` modifier; and the
missing `E37` error code.

The version table gains the five datestamps whose features are now
actually dissected — 20150617, 20191015, 20200226, 20250523 and
20260306. Nothing is advertised that isn't implemented.

The unofficial "protocol type" `P` modifier is dropped. It came from
erlrtpproxy, never shipped there, and erlrtpproxy is now EOL — nothing
ever put it on the wire, and RTPproxy has since given `P` a meaning of
its own, which the following commit implements. This removes the
`rtpproxy.command_parameter_proto` field.

### RTPproxy-ng

The info column carried the entire bencoded payload, SDP and all —
hundreds of unreadable characters per packet. Every ng message names
itself, so the `command`, `result` and `call-id` are now picked out of
the top level dictionary (nested keys are stepped over, never mistaken
for the real one) and the column reads `Request: offer, Call-ID: ...`.
`rtpproxy.ng.command == "delete"` is filterable.

That also made request/reply tracking possible: `rtpproxy_add_tid()` was
only ever reached by the plain protocol, so ng exchanges had no
"Response in", no round trip time, and nothing tying a reply to its
call. They do now.

Finally the session description is handed to the SDP dissector, so
rtpengine's rewriting is visible as structured fields — in the included
capture the offer names 192.168.0.1:8000 and the reply to it
192.168.0.101:37506. As with SDP carried over any other protocol, this
also sets up the media streams it describes.

### Testing

Six tests in `test/suite_dissection.py`, four capture files. The first
commit is a 2021 test addition that was never submitted; the two new
captures cover the ng error/warning replies and a reply large enough to
be split across two IP fragments, which arrive out of order.

**The two new captures are sanitised real traffic** — addresses rewritten
to RFC 1918 in the packet headers *and* inside the bencoded payloads,
and MAC addresses replaced. Replacements were chosen with identical
string lengths so the fragment offsets and bencode length prefixes stay
valid.

`tools/check_apis.py` and `tools/check_typed_item_calls.py` report no
warnings. Beyond the suite, this was run over ~23k frames of real
rtpengine traffic and several fuzz corpora with no dissector exceptions,
and against the unmodified dissector to confirm frame counts and decoded
content are otherwise unchanged.

Assisted-by: Claude

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Hand the RTPproxy-ng session description to the SDP dissector
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Hand the RTPproxy-ng session description to the SDP dissector

The whole point of an "offer" or an "answer" is the session description
it carries, and rtpengine rewrites the addresses and ports in it - which
is exactly what one opens such a capture to look at. It was shown as one
long bencode string.

It is just another string as far as bencode is concerned, so pass it on
to the dissector which understands it. The rewriting is then plain to
see: the offer names 192.168.0.1:8000 and the reply to it 192.168.0.101:
37506.

Note that this also sets up the media streams the description names, the
way SDP carried over any other protocol does, so RTP in the same capture
gets decoded.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Track RTPproxy-ng requests and replies
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Track RTPproxy-ng requests and replies

rtpproxy_add_tid() was only ever reached by the plain protocol, so an
RTPproxy-ng exchange got no request/response matching at all - no
"Response in", no round trip time, and a reply that showed nothing to
tie it to the call it belonged to.

Now that a message says whether it carries a "command" or a "result"
there is enough to pair the two up by cookie, exactly as the plain
protocol does. The Call-ID of the request is remembered, so a reply -
which carries none of its own - can show it as a generated field.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Name the RTPproxy-ng command and result
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Name the RTPproxy-ng command and result

The info column carried the whole bencoded payload, SDP and all, which
on a busy capture is several hundred unreadable characters per packet
and says nothing about what the message actually is.

Every ng message names itself: a request carries a "command" key, a
reply a "result" one. Pick those out, along with the "call-id", and let
the column say "Request: offer, Call-ID: ..." or "Reply: error". They
are dissected as fields as well, so "rtpproxy.ng.command == \"delete\""
now works, and the Call-ID reuses the field the plain protocol already
had.

Only the top level dictionary is searched - the keys of a nested one are
stepped over, so a "command" inside it is never mistaken for the one
naming the message.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Add a test capture for a reassembled RTPproxy-ng reply
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Add a test capture for a reassembled RTPproxy-ng reply

A reply to a "query" easily outgrows the MTU, and the two fragments do
not necessarily arrive in order - in this capture the second one comes
first. Nothing exercised that path, even though it is the one where a
bencoded payload reaches the dissector as a reassembled buffer rather
than as a datagram.

Taken from a real exchange; the addresses, both in the packet headers
and inside the bencoded payloads, and the MAC addresses have been
rewritten to RFC 1918 / locally administered ones. Rewriting the ones
carried by a fragment required replacements of exactly the same length,
so that the fragment offsets kept lining up.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Add a test capture for the RTPproxy-ng error replies
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Add a test capture for the RTPproxy-ng error replies

The two captures the suite had both carry a well formed request; nothing
covered what rtpengine answers with when it refuses one. This one holds
an "offer" rejected with "error"/"error-reason: Unknown call-id" and a
"delete" answered with "result: ok" alongside a "warning", which is the
combination the reply parser is most likely to get wrong.

Taken from a real exchange; the addresses, both in the packet headers
and inside the bencoded payloads, and the MAC addresses have been
rewritten to RFC 1918 / locally administered ones.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the reply to a "Q" command
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the reply to a "Q" command

A query is answered with the counters it asked for, or with a fixed set
of five when it named none. Neither was dissected: a plain reply
("60 1200 1198 2398 2") went through the port-and-address parser of an
offer reply and produced a bad IPv4 address, and a verbose one
("ttl=60 npkts_ina=1200 ...") was not recognized at all.

A reply carries no hint of the command it belongs to, and the verbose
form may start with something that looks like one - "ndropped=0" was
dissected as an "N" command - so remember the command each cookie stood
for and look it up when the reply arrives. The counter names a query
asked for are remembered along with it, which is what makes the plain
form readable: the values are matched against them by position, falling
back to the five defaults.

The counters are registered with the types RTPproxy prints them with, so
that they can be filtered on and graphed - "rtpproxy.counter.ndropped >
0" and the like. Anything not recognized, or not parsable as the type it
should be, is kept as a string rather than dropped.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the counter names of a "Q" command
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the counter names of a "Q" command

"Q[v] call_id from_tag to_tag [counter1 ... counterN]" may name the
counters it wants back, but the dissector stopped right after the tags
and left them undissected.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the official "P" command modifier
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the official "P" command modifier

Since the 20250523 protocol version the "C" command takes a "P"
modifier, which asks RTPproxy to reply with the address and port it has
allocated for the recording stream instead of a plain OK. It is only
accepted by "C", and only when the recording target is a remote one
("udp:host:port") - "R" and a local target are rejected outright.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Drop the unofficial "protocol type" command modifier
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Drop the unofficial "protocol type" command modifier

The "P" modifier was dissected as an RTP transmission protocol selector
(UDP/TCP/SCTP) taken from erlrtpproxy. It never made it into erlrtpproxy
though, and erlrtpproxy itself has since been EOLed, so nothing has ever
put such a modifier on the wire.

RTPproxy in the meantime gave "P" a meaning of its own, which the next
commit implements, so retire the extension along with its
"rtpproxy.command_parameter_proto" field rather than let the two clash.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the "%%CC_SELF%%" notify address wildcard
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the "%%CC_SELF%%" notify address wildcard

Since the 20150617 protocol version the host part of a notification
target may be the "%%CC_SELF%%" wildcard, which asks RTPproxy to send
the notification back to whoever the command came from. It used to be
run through the IPv4 parser and reported as a bad address.

The address taken from ip.src/ipv6.src is now shown as a generated item
the same way it already is for a target carrying a bare port number.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect all the notify socket forms
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect all the notify socket forms

The notification target of an "U" command was always run through the
ip:port parser, but RTPproxy accepts a local socket just as well - as
"unix:<path>", or as a bare path for compatibility with the 1.0-2.0
releases - and spells an INET one "tcp:<host>:<port>". A socket path was
therefore reported as a bad IPv4 address followed by port 0, and the
"tcp:" prefix turned the address into a bad IPv6 one by adding a colon.

Recognize the prefixes, tell a path from a bare port number the way
RTPproxy does, and accept an IPv6 address enclosed in square brackets.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Stop parsing a command once its arguments run out
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Stop parsing a command once its arguments run out

The whole request path walked the arguments with unbounded searches -
tvb_find_uint8_remaining() and tvb_skip_wsp() over the captured length -
and never compared the result against the end of the command. A command
carrying fewer arguments than its syntax allows therefore kept going
past its own end: the offset ran beyond realsize, "end - begin" wrapped
around in rtpproxy_add_tag() and the packet was reported as malformed.

"U call_id 192.168.0.1 10000" was enough to trigger it, and so was every
other truncated command - a fairly common sight, since a control socket
datagram is quite happily cut short by a broken SIP proxy.

Bound every field to the command instead, and bail out cleanly as soon
as there is nothing left to dissect. Two more reads off the end go with
it: the zero length Media-ID placeholder was anchored just past the tag,
which is outside of the tvb when the command carries no trailing LF, and
the "sessions ..." reply detection looked at the second byte of a
command which may well be one byte long ("S").

Over a corpus of 1604 generated commands this takes the number of
dissector exceptions from 969 down to zero.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the address label of the "L" command modifier
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the address label of the "L" command modifier

Since the 20260306 protocol version the "L" modifier of the "U"/"L"
commands takes a bind address label in curly braces instead of an
address, so that the caller doesn't have to know the addresses RTPproxy
is bound to. "Ul{ext}" used to be walked byte by byte, with "e" reported
as an "external network" request and "t" as a transcoding one.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect IPv6 addresses of the "L"/"R" command modifiers
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect IPv6 addresses of the "L"/"R" command modifiers

RTPproxy accepts an IPv6 address enclosed in square brackets everywhere
it accepts an IPv4 one, but both modifiers only ever scanned for digits
and dots. "Ul[2001:db8::1]" was therefore torn apart byte by byte, each
of them reported as a command modifier of its own - and "db" happened to
look like a DTMF payload ID followed by a brief stats request.

Factor the address out of the two nearly identical branches and teach it
about the bracketed form. The "no address at all" case keeps adding no
subtree, since a bare "L" is the "load average" modifier of the "I"
command rather than a local address.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Don't read past a command modifier without a value
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Don't read past a command modifier without a value

The "P" (protocol type) and "U" (accounting) modifiers both consume one
more byte, but neither checked that the byte is actually there. A command
ending right after such a modifier - "CP call_id target from_tag" for
instance - was reported as a "[Malformed Packet]".

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the "&&" sub-commands
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the "&&" sub-commands

Since the 20191015 protocol version an "U", "L" or "Q" command may be
followed by any number of sub-commands separated by a standalone "&&"
argument, and the reply carries one result per sub-command.

The dissector knew nothing about them, so the separator and everything
behind it were consumed by the positional parser of the main command -
"U ... from_tag && M0" reported "&&" as the to_tag. A reply consisting
of a port and a result only ("12345 && 0") went as far as running the
result through the IPv4 parser and complaining about a bad address.

Cut the trailer off before the command is parsed and dissect it on its
own afterwards. The separator is recognized the way RTPproxy itself
does it - as a whitespace delimited "&&" argument - so that a Call-ID or
a tag containing "&&" is left alone.

The bencode sniffing test is factored out into a helper, both because
the new code needs it and because it used to read two bytes past the
command without checking that they are actually there.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Recognize the "v" (verbose) command modifier
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Recognize the "v" (verbose) command modifier

Both "G[v]" and "Q[v]" ask for a verbose reply, but the modifier was not
listed, so it was reported as "Parameter: Unknown ('v')".

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Add the missing E37 error code
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Add the missing E37 error code

ECODE_INVLARG_7 is returned when the remote address of an "U"/"L"
command cannot be resolved. It was the only gap left in the error table.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Fix extraction of the second tag
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Fix extraction of the second tag

rtpproxy_add_tag() already leaves the offset on the separator following
the tag it has just consumed, but the caller went on to recompute the
offset from new_offset - which had last been set while looking for the
Call-ID. The second tag was therefore parsed starting at the first one
again, so "D call_id from_tag to_tag" reported "from_tag" twice and the
to_tag was never shown.

Advance from the offset rtpproxy_add_tag() returns instead. While at it,
honour its return value for the second tag as well: without a to_tag the
dissector fell through to the notification address parser and reported
the from_tag as a notify target of an "U" command.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Fix the length passed to tvb_find_uint8_length()
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Fix the length passed to tvb_find_uint8_length()

The third argument of tvb_find_uint8_length() is the number of bytes to
scan, but all the three call sites handed it "end" - an absolute offset
into the tvb. The searches therefore ran way past the field they were
supposed to look at, up to the end of the captured data.

For a tag without a Media-ID this made the search fail with new_offset
pointing just past the last scanned byte, and the "<skipped>" Media-ID
placeholder was then anchored at new_offset+1, i.e. outside of the tvb.
Every session command carrying a tag - D, R, N, U, L, P, C, Q - ended up
as a "[Malformed Packet]" because of that. A stray semicolon anywhere
later in the packet was mis-detected as this tag's separator as well,
and in the notify address parser a colon belonging to another field made
an IPv4 address look like an IPv6 one.

Pass the actual field lengths instead.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the "N" (stop recording) command
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the "N" (stop recording) command

"N[a] call_id from_tag [to_tag]" has the very same shape as the other
session commands, so it only needs to be listed in the command table and
routed through the generic request path. The "a" modifier selects all
the recordings rather than an asymmetric stream here, so mention both
meanings the way the other overloaded modifiers already do.

Advertise the matching "20200226" protocol version now that the command
is actually dissected.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Dissect the "G" (get statistics) command
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Dissect the "G" (get statistics) command

The "G" command was not recognized at all, so such packets were shown as
a bare cookie with no request tree and took no part in the request/reply
tracking.

Add it to the command table and dissect its optional list of the
requested counter names ("G[v] [stat_name1 ... stat_nameN]"). Unlike the
other commands "G" may carry no arguments whatsoever, so the modifiers
are looked up within the command boundaries only - otherwise a bare "G"
would report the trailing LF as a command parameter.

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>

commits_data.title: RTPproxy: Add basic unit-tests
commits_data.message:
RTPproxy: Add basic unit-tests

Assisted-by: Claude
Signed-off-by: Peter Lemenkov <lemenkov@gmail.com>
